q: How are a refinery's emissions split between diesel, naphtha, polymers and other products?
title: Refinery emissions: splitting by product
short: There is no single answer. Standards prefer splitting by process unit first, then allocating what is left by a physical measure such as mass or energy content, and only then by price. The method changes each product's figure a lot, so a supplier's number is only comparable if you know which rule it used.
audience: Buyers of fuels, naphtha, polypropylene and other refinery products, and refinery sustainability teams answering them

ol: Avoid allocation where you can: assign each process unit's fuel and process emissions to the streams it actually makes.
Where units make several products, split by a physical relationship such as mass or energy content.
Use economic value only when no physical relationship fits, and say so.

sections.h: Why it matters to a buyer
p: A lubricant base oil or a polymer grade can carry very different figures under mass, energy or value allocation. Two refineries quoting different numbers may simply be using different rules, not running cleaner plants.

ul: The allocation method and the boundary (gate of refinery or of the product plant).
The year and whether captive power and steam are inside.
Whether crude production and shipping are included upstream.

senseible: Senseible reads the invoices for the products you buy into a dated, fingerprinted record, so a supplier figure and the quantity it applies to can be traced back to the documents behind it. It does not calculate refinery allocations.

sources.label: GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard
